controls.statement: RHEL 9 is a controlled platform for building an ISMS scope; organizational scoping, asset inventory, and governance remain customer responsibilities. Product documentation supports security-relevant deployment and lifecycle practices.

Regulatory and contractual requirements are interpreted and applied by the customer; RHEL provides configurable technical controls (audit, crypto, identity, MAC) to help meet common obligations when properly deployed.
Policies and procedures are owned by the institution; RHEL supplies security hardening guides, crypto frameworks, and automation-friendly interfaces (e.g. OpenSCAP, system roles).
Management commitment and roles are organizational; RHEL supports delegated administration (sudo, RBAC integrations via SSSD) consistent with customer-defined roles.
Risk treatment plans are customer-owned; RHEL offers documented hardening paths and compliance-oriented profiles in scap-security-guide to reduce technical risk when selected and applied.
Third-party and supply-chain governance is shared: Red Hat signs content and publishes errata; customers verify signatures and subscribe to update channels appropriate to their assurance needs.
Incident handling processes are organizational; RHEL provides auditd, journaling, and integrations for centralized logging when configured by the customer.
Business continuity is customer-designed; RHEL supports backup-friendly storage, high-availability patterns, and reproducible configuration via automation.
Data protection impact and privacy engineering are contextual; RHEL provides disk encryption (LUKS), TLS stacks, and MAC (SELinux) as technical building blocks.
Awareness and training are organizational; Red Hat documents security features so administrators can operate RHEL consistently with institutional standards.
Network segmentation and zoning are implemented with customer topology; RHEL provides firewalld, nftables, and routing features to enforce host-level network policy.
Remote access controls depend on customer services; RHEL ships OpenSSH and PAM, configurable to disallow root login, enforce key-based auth, and integrate with enterprise identity.
RHEL 9 includes SELinux (MAC) and documented policies; enforcing mode is supported and recommended for many deployments when compatible with workloads.
Malware mitigation combines customer process with technical controls: package signing, minimal installation, and Security-Enhanced Linux reduce exposure; additional AV/EDR is customer-chosen.
Patch and vulnerability management uses customer processes; RHEL provides dnf, Red Hat Errata, and tools to evaluate system security posture (OpenSCAP) when installed.
Secure configuration baselines can be applied using scap-security-guide profiles, system roles, or image builders; the exact baseline is customer-selected.
Logging and monitoring use auditd, systemd journal, and rsyslog; forwarding to SIEM is customer-configured.
Time synchronization for audit correlation is typically provided by chrony; customers point strata to trusted time sources.

gaps: Mappings are indicative, not exhaustive legal interpretations of Grundschutz++ requirements.
Several GC.* controls are primarily organizational; implementation-status stays partial by design.
Rule IDs reference ComplianceAsCode / scap-security-guide naming; profile selection (e.g. OSPP) changes rule applicability.
OpenSCAP evaluation in CI uses a Fedora-hosted data stream; results validate check wiring, not a certified assessment.
